1	# Part 3 — Full stack app
2	
3	Parts 1 and 2 told you what to build. This one doesn't.
4	
5	**Build a full stack app that helps someone understand Chapter 99.** What that
6	means is your call. We are building in a complex domain, with experts dedicating
7	entire careers to understanding the ins and outs of the HTS code. Build something
8	that explains how tariffs work to a novice.
9	
10	**Think of yourself as the primary user.** Not a hypothetical importer, not us —
11	you. What presentation would have made this domain click faster? Where did you have
12	to hold five things in your head at once because nothing showed them together?
13	That confusion is your product spec.
14	
15	**Speed is part of the design.** The data does not change until the next revision.
16	So you can compute an answer once and store it, instead of making the database work
17	it out again on every request. Build the tables your screens need: flatten a join,
18	add a materialized view, precompute the exclusion graph, store a derived column.
19	
20	The hard part is choosing. What is worth storing, and how do you keep it true when
21	the tables under it change? Write down what you picked and why in `SUBMISSION.md`.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Getting started
26	
27	There's a bare scaffold in [`app/`](../app/README.md) — one route, one query, no
28	framework. It exists so you don't spend your first twenty minutes on connection
29	strings.
30	
31	```bash
32	./dev.sh                  # from the repo root → http://localhost:3000
33	```
34	
35	[`AGENTS.md`](../AGENTS.md) has the stack in full — services, ports, and how to
36	run the app on your host instead of in a container.
37	
38	Delete it if it's in your way. The only thing we ask is that
39	`SUBMISSION.md` tells us how to run what you built.
40	
41	---
42	
43	## Additional resources
44	
45	**Where a Chapter 99 line comes from.** A trade action starts as a presidential
46	proclamation or a USTR notice, gets published in the **Federal Register**, and
47	lands in the HTSUS as new 9903 headings. **CBP** then tells filers how to actually
48	enter the goods via a **CSMS** message. So a single duty has three artifacts: the
49	legal instrument, the tariff line, and the filing instruction. Our dataset only
50	has the middle one.
51	
52	| Source                                                                              | What's there                                                                                         | How to read it                                      |
53	| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
54	| [**Federal Register**](https://www.federalregister.gov/)                            | The legal instrument — proclamations and USTR notices that create, amend, or terminate 9903 headings | Open JSON API, no key                               |
55	| [**USITC HTS**](https://hts.usitc.gov/)                                             | The tariff schedule itself, plus revision history and the notes PDFs                                 | Same `reststop` API you're already using            |
56	| [**CBP CSMS**](https://www.cbp.gov/trade/automated/cargo-systems-messaging-service) | Filing instructions — stacking order, which 9903 code goes on which line, effective dates            | Web archive + email list; no clean API              |
57	| [**CBP CROSS**](https://rulings.cbp.gov/)                                           | Binding rulings: how CBP classified a specific real product                                          | JSON search API, no key                             |
58	| [**USITC DataWeb**](https://dataweb.usitc.gov/)                                     | Actual import volumes and duties collected, by HTS code                                              | Free account; API key for bulk                      |
59	| [**eCFR Title 19**](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-19)                          | The customs regulations themselves                                                                   | Open API, no key — XML for text, JSON for structure |
60	
61	### Programmatic access
62	
63	The Federal Register API is the most useful of these and needs no key. Filter by
64	agency and type — a bare `"section 301"` term search returns mostly unrelated
65	documents, since §301 also numbers a Clean Water Act provision:
66	
67	```bash
68	# Recent USTR notices — where Section 301 actions are announced.
69	# Brackets are percent-encoded because curl treats [] as a glob.
70	curl -s -A 'your-app/1.0 (you@example.com)' \
71	  'https://www.federalregister.gov/api/v1/documents.json?per_page=5&order=newest&conditions%5Bagencies%5D%5B%5D=trade-representative-office-of-united-states&conditions%5Btype%5D%5B%5D=NOTICE&fields%5B%5D=title&fields%5B%5D=publication_date&fields%5B%5D=html_url'
72	```
73	
74	The HTS API tells you which revision you're looking at.
75	
76	```bash
77	curl -s 'https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/currentRelease'
78	# → {"name":"2026HTSRev15","title":"Revision 15 (2026)"}   # as of 2026-08-03
79	
80	# Keyword search across the schedule, same shape as the bulk export
81	curl -s 'https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/search?keyword=laptop'
82	```
83	
84	CROSS returns a `tariffs` array on every ruling, which makes it joinable to your
85	data — and those arrays often contain 9903 codes, so a ruling can show you a real
86	product with its Chapter 99 treatment already attached:
87	
88	```bash
89	curl -s 'https://rulings.cbp.gov/api/search?term=laptop%20backpack&pageSize=5'
90	# → "tariffs": ["4202.92.3120", ..., "9903.88.03"]
91	```
92	
93	eCFR serves regulation text as XML, and the table of contents as JSON:
94	
95	```bash
96	# Full text of 19 CFR 141 (entry of merchandise) — XML only, .json returns 406
97	curl -s 'https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-01-01/title-19.xml?part=141'
98	
99	# Structure of Title 19, for finding the part you want
100	curl -s 'https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/structure/2026-01-01/title-19.json'
101	```
102	
103	### By hand
104	
105	- **Federal Register** — search by agency ("Trade Representative"), or browse
106	  [presidential documents](https://www.federalregister.gov/presidential-documents/executive-orders)
107	  for proclamations. Each document links its own RIN and docket.
108	- **CSMS** — the [archive](https://www.cbp.gov/trade/automated/cargo-systems-messaging-service)
109	  is paginated and JS-rendered, so it doesn't scrape cleanly; read it in a browser.
110	  Messages are the fastest way to understand _stacking order_, which the HTSUS
111	  itself never states.
112	- **CROSS** — search a product description in plain English. Rulings show the
113	  reasoning, which is often the only place a classification boundary is explained.
114	- **regulations.gov** — public comment dockets for pending actions. The API needs
115	  a [free api.data.gov key](https://api.data.gov/signup/); the web UI doesn't.
116	
117	---
118	
119	Back to: [the main README](../README.md)

"""
A workflow that takes an input and returns an output. That's all it does.

It exists to prove your worker is connected and running tasks, and to show the
shape of a Hatchet workflow. Delete it once you have a real one.

    python -m echo_run "some text"
"""

from hatchet_sdk import Context, Hatchet
from pydantic import BaseModel

hatchet = Hatchet()


class EchoInput(BaseModel):
    message: str


class EchoOutput(BaseModel):
    message: str
    length: int


echo_workflow = hatchet.workflow(
    name="Echo",
    input_validator=EchoInput,
)


# The return type hint is what gives you a validated, typed result on the
# other end — without it you get a plain dict back.
@echo_workflow.task()
def echo(input: EchoInput, ctx: Context) -> EchoOutput:
    ctx.log(f"received: {input.message}")
    return EchoOutput(message=input.message, length=len(input.message))

"""
Trigger the Echo workflow and print what comes back.

    uv run python -m echo_run "hello"

Needs the worker running in another terminal.
"""

import sys

from echo import EchoInput, EchoOutput, echo_workflow


def main() -> None:
    message = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "hello"

    # Blocks until the run finishes. Use `wait_for_result=False` for a handle
    # you can poll instead.
    result = echo_workflow.run(EchoInput(message=message))

    # Results come back keyed by task name.
    output = EchoOutput.model_validate(result["echo"])
    print(f"message={output.message!r} length={output.length}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Workflows

Your Hatchet workflows go here. Ships with one that does nothing useful, so you
can confirm the plumbing works before writing the scraper.

## Setup

`./dev.sh` from the repo root runs a worker for you, in a container, and restarts
it when you edit a `.py` here. Trigger a run against it from this directory:

```bash
cd workflows && uv sync
uv run python -m echo_run "hello chapter 99"
# → message='hello chapter 99' length=16
```

To run the worker on your host instead, don't use `./dev.sh` — start just the
infrastructure, then the worker yourself:

```bash
docker compose up -d        # from the repo root; wait for hatchet to be healthy
cd workflows && uv sync
uv run python -m worker     # one terminal: registers workflows, waits for work
uv run python -m echo_run "hello chapter 99"   # another
```

**Run one worker at a time.** They share the token in `.env`, so a host worker
and the container worker will both register and Hatchet will hand tasks to
whichever it picks — including the one running code you didn't just edit.

Runs show up in the Hatchet UI at http://localhost:8080 — no login, it opens
straight to the dashboard. Workflows can be triggered from the UI or
programatically.

## The worker in Docker

`./dev.sh` is the short version. For the worker alone:

```bash
docker compose --profile worker watch    # foreground, restarts on edit
docker compose --profile worker up -d    # detached, no reload
docker compose logs -f worker
```

Either bind-mounts `./workflows`. Under `watch`, editing a `.py` restarts the
worker for you; adding a dependency to `pyproject.toml` restarts it too, picking
up the new package via `uv sync`. Detached, you restart it yourself with
`docker compose restart worker`.

Either path is fine. Host-running gives you a debugger; the container gives you
one less thing to install and the reload for free. Note that from inside the
container your database is `db:5432`, not `localhost:5432` — the service reads
`DATABASE_URL` from the environment for exactly this reason.

## What's here

| File          |                                                             |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `echo.py`     | A workflow with one task: takes an input, returns an output |
| `worker.py`   | The worker process. Register your workflows here            |
| `echo_run.py` | Triggers a run and prints the result                        |
| `.env`        | Hatchet connection settings. Committed — see below          |

## The shape of a workflow

```python
class EchoInput(BaseModel):
    message: str

class EchoOutput(BaseModel):
    message: str
    length: int

echo_workflow = hatchet.workflow(name="Echo", input_validator=EchoInput)

@echo_workflow.task()
def echo(input: EchoInput, ctx: Context) -> EchoOutput:
    return EchoOutput(message=input.message, length=len(input.message))
```

[Hatchet docs](https://docs.hatchet.run/home/setup) is a great resource for
documentation and patterns.

## Notes

**Register your workflows in `worker.py`.** If you forget, the engine will accept
a run and it'll sit queued forever with nothing to pick it up. This is the most
common way to lose ten minutes here.

**The token in `.env` is committed, and that's deliberate.** We run the Hatchet
dev image, which has auth compiled out — no login on the dashboard, and one fixed
non-expiring worker token that's the same on every auth-disabled instance. It
isn't a secret and it survives `./cleanup.sh`, so there's no setup step and
nothing to rotate. Don't copy the pattern into anything real.

-- Chapter 99 — starting schema.
--
-- Script to seed database schema. Add columns, tables, etc as needed.
-- Should be runnable from a clean install. Should define the schema
-- needed for parts 1, 2, and 3.
--
-- Rerunnable: it drops what it creates first, so applying it twice is safe.
-- Postgres has no CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE, so a clean schema means dropping.
-- That also means applying this wipes your parsed data; it is a schema reset,
-- not a migration.
--
--   ./setup.sh
--
-- Order matters on the way down: rule_edge references rule.

BEGIN;

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS rule_edge CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS rule CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS hts_base CASCADE;

-- Chapters 1-97: what Chapter 99 points back at.
CREATE TABLE hts_base (
  hts          text PRIMARY KEY,
  description  text,
  mfn_rate_pct numeric
);

-- Chapter 99 provisions. rate_kind is the operator, rate_value the operand:
-- 'additive' with 25 means "base rate + 25", which a single numeric column
-- could not express.
CREATE TABLE rule (
  hts         text PRIMARY KEY,
  subchapter  text NOT NULL,
  description text NOT NULL,
  rate_kind   text NOT NULL
    CHECK (rate_kind IN ('free','additive','ad_valorem','no_change','specific','other')),
  rate_value  numeric,
  note_ref    text
);

-- The two relationships Chapter 99 states in prose.
--
-- target_hts is deliberately not a foreign key: a provision can name a base
-- code that no longer exists in the current revision, and those are worth
-- recording rather than dropping.
CREATE TABLE rule_edge (
  source_hts text NOT NULL REFERENCES rule(hts) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  edge_type  text NOT NULL CHECK (edge_type IN ('references','excludes')),
  target_hts text NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (source_hts, edge_type, target_hts)
);

CREATE INDEX rule_edge_target_idx ON rule_edge (target_hts, edge_type);

COMMIT;

services:
  # ============================================
  # Your application database.
  # This is where your Chapter 99 tables go.
  # Reachable from your host on localhost:5432
  # and from other containers as db:5432
  #
  # Everything is published on the stock ports, so
  # stop anything already on 5432/8080/3000 first.
  # ============================================
  db:
    image: postgres:16.3
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: postgres
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
      POSTGRES_DB: chp99
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10

  # ============================================
  # Hatchet Lite - workflow orchestration
  #
  #   Admin UI : http://localhost:8080   (no login)
  #   gRPC     : localhost:7077
  #
  # This is the -dev image, which has authentication
  # compiled out: the dashboard opens straight up,
  # no login. Workers still authenticate over gRPC,
  # but the image ships one fixed non-expiring token
  # that's committed in workflows/.env — so there is
  # nothing to set up.
  #
  # Uses PostgreSQL as its message queue rather than
  # RabbitMQ. Slower under real load, but one less
  # service to run for a take-home.
  #
  # Docs: https://docs.hatchet.run/self-hosting/hatchet-lite
  # ============================================
  hatchet:
    image: ghcr.io/hatchet-dev/hatchet/hatchet-lite-dev:v0.94.10
    ports:
      - "8080:8888"
      - "7077:7077"
    depends_on:
      hatchet_db:
        condition: service_healthy
    volumes:
      - hatchet_lite_config:/config
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:postgres@hatchet_db:5432/hatchet_db?sslmode=disable
      - SERVER_MSGQUEUE_KIND=postgres

      - SERVER_URL=http://localhost:8080
      - SERVER_GRPC_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0
      - SERVER_GRPC_INSECURE=t
      # Handed out in the token, and dialed by the server's own API. Published
      # as 7077:7077 so one value works from both sides: host workers reach it
      # through the port mapping, the in-container dial finds 7077 bound.
      - SERVER_GRPC_BROADCAST_ADDRESS=localhost:7077
      - SERVER_GRPC_PORT=7077

      # Auth is compiled out of this image, but the config still generates
      # cookie secrets, and hatchet-admin needs them to mint worker tokens.
      - SERVER_AUTH_COOKIE_DOMAIN=localhost
      - SERVER_AUTH_COOKIE_INSECURE=t

      - SERVER_LOGGER_LEVEL=error
      - SERVER_LOGGER_FORMAT=console
      - DATABASE_LOGGER_LEVEL=warn
      - DATABASE_LOGGER_FORMAT=console
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8888/api/ready"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 12
      start_period: 45s
    restart: unless-stopped

  # ============================================
  # Your Hatchet worker.
  #
  #   docker compose --profile worker up -d
  #   docker compose logs -f worker
  #
  # Bind-mounts ./workflows. Run it with
  #
  #   docker compose --profile worker watch
  #
  # and edits to .py files restart the worker for
  # you — Python caches imported modules, so a
  # long-running worker otherwise keeps serving the
  # old code with no error to tell you. Opt-in, like
  # the app service — running it on your host gives
  # you a faster loop and a debugger.
  # See workflows/README.md.
  # ============================================
  worker:
    profiles: ["worker"]
    image: python:3.11-slim
    working_dir: /workflows
    # uv is installed into the image on start; the venv lives in a named volume
    # so it survives restarts and stays off the bind mount.
    command: >
      sh -c "pip install --quiet --root-user-action=ignore uv &&
             uv sync &&
             uv run python -m worker"
    depends_on:
      hatchet:
        condition: service_healthy
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    env_file:
      # Committed to the repo — the dev image's fixed worker token is not a
      # secret. See the comments in that file.
      - ./workflows/.env
    environment:
      # The broadcast address is localhost:7077, which from inside a container
      # points at the container itself. Override it to the service name.
      HATCHET_CLIENT_HOST_PORT: hatchet:7077
      HATCHET_CLIENT_TLS_STRATEGY: none
      # Your data lives here, not on localhost:5432, once you're on the network.
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:postgres@db:5432/chp99
      # Venv on a named volume, off the bind mount, so it can't collide with a
      # .venv you built on the host.
      UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT: /venv
      # The volume and the mount are different filesystems, so hardlinking fails.
      UV_LINK_MODE: copy
      # Where to put downloads. Same path in the container as on your host, so a
      # scraper writing here works either way.
      DATA_DIR: /data
    volumes:
      - ./workflows:/workflows
      - worker_venv:/venv
      # Downloads survive the container and are visible on your host.
      - ./data:/data
    restart: unless-stopped
    # `docker compose --profile worker watch` acts on these; a plain `up` ignores
    # them, so the service behaves exactly as before if you don't opt in.
    develop:
      watch:
        # Editing a workflow restarts the process, which is what clears Python's
        # module cache. The bind mount above already makes the file visible.
        - action: restart
          path: ./workflows
          target: /workflows
          include: ["**/*.py"]
          ignore: ["**/__pycache__/**", ".venv/**"]
        # A new dependency needs `uv sync`, which runs in the start command --
        # so restarting is enough here too. (`rebuild` needs a build context,
        # and this service runs a stock image.)
        - action: restart
          path: ./workflows/pyproject.toml
          target: /workflows/pyproject.toml

  # ============================================
  # The Part 3 scaffold, containerized.
  #
  #   docker compose --profile app up -d
  #   → http://localhost:3000
  #
  # Opt-in, because running it on your host is the
  # smoother path — bind-mounted node_modules and
  # file watching are both slower in a container,
  # especially on macOS. See app/README.md.
  #
  # If you replace the scaffold with another stack,
  # rewrite or delete this service. It is not load-
  # bearing for anything else in the compose file.
  # ============================================
  app:
    profiles: ["app"]
    image: oven/bun:1.3.3-alpine
    working_dir: /app
    command: bun dev
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      # db:5432 rather than localhost:5432 — we're on the compose network here.
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:postgres@db:5432/chp99
      PORT: 3000
    volumes:
      - ./app:/app
      # Keeps container deps off the bind mount, so they don't collide with
      # whatever your host installed.
      - app_node_modules:/app/node_modules

  # Hatchet's internal database. Not for your data.
  hatchet_db:
    image: postgres:16.3
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: postgres
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
      POSTGRES_DB: hatchet_db
    volumes:
      - hatchet_postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10

volumes:
  postgres_data:
  hatchet_postgres_data:
  hatchet_lite_config:
  app_node_modules:
  worker_venv:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Start the whole stack with hot reload.
#
#   ./dev.sh
#
# Brings up Postgres, Hatchet, the worker and the app, then watches
# ./workflows for changes. Editing any .py restarts the worker, which is what
# clears Python's module cache -- a worker left running after an edit keeps
# serving the old code and the run succeeds with stale results, with no error
# to tell you.
#
# Why a script: `watch` is a CLI mode, not something the compose file can turn
# on, and the worker and app are opt-in profiles. This is the one command that
# combines them.
#
# Runs in the foreground and streams logs. Ctrl-C stops watching and stops the
# containers.

set -euo pipefail

cd "$(dirname "$0")"

# Ports we publish. Checked up front because the failure is otherwise a wall of
# compose output ending in "address already in use".
#
# Skipped when our own stack is already up: compose recreates those containers
# itself, and the ports it is holding are not a conflict.
if [ -z "$(docker compose ps -q 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
  check_port() {
    if lsof -nP -iTCP:"$1" -sTCP:LISTEN >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      echo "port $1 ($2) is already in use:" >&2
      lsof -nP -iTCP:"$1" -sTCP:LISTEN 2>/dev/null | tail -n +2 | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
      return 1
    fi
  }

  busy=0
  check_port 5432 postgres || busy=1
  check_port 8080 "hatchet UI" || busy=1
  check_port 7077 "hatchet gRPC" || busy=1
  check_port 3000 app || busy=1

  if [ "$busy" -ne 0 ]; then
    echo >&2
    echo "Stop whatever is holding those ports and try again." >&2
    exit 1
  fi
fi

echo "starting db, hatchet, worker, app -- Ctrl-C to stop"
echo

# --watch implies up. Both profiles, so a plain ./dev.sh is the whole stack.
exec docker compose --profile worker --profile app up --watch

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Apply db/schema.sql to the chp99 database.
#
#   ./setup.sh                 apply db/schema.sql
#   ./setup.sh path/to.sql     apply something else
#
# Safe to run twice: the schema drops what it creates before creating it. That
# also means it wipes parsed data — it is a schema reset, not a migration.
#
# Needs the stack up (./dev.sh). Runs psql inside the db container, so you don't
# need a local postgres client.

set -euo pipefail

cd "$(dirname "$0")"

SCHEMA="${1:-db/schema.sql}"

if [ ! -f "$SCHEMA" ]; then
  echo "no such file: $SCHEMA" >&2
  exit 1
fi

if [ -z "$(docker compose ps -q db 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
  echo "the db container isn't running — start the stack first:" >&2
  echo "  ./dev.sh" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# ON_ERROR_STOP so a failure exits non-zero instead of scrolling past.
docker compose exec -T db \
  psql -U postgres -d chp99 -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -q < "$SCHEMA"

echo "applied $SCHEMA"
docker compose exec -T db psql -U postgres -d chp99 -c '\dt'

I've read through the whole repo. Here's my understanding of the task:

## What this is
A take-home for Pax AI: build a pipeline that ingests the US Harmonized Tariff Schedule's "Chapter 99" (temporary trade actions — Section 301/232 tariffs, IEEPA actions, duty suspensions) and makes it understandable. Chapter 99 doesn't classify goods itself — it modifies duties on goods classified elsewhere (chapters 1-97), via prose cross-references like *"provided for in subheading 2922.49.30"* and exclusion chains like *"except for products described in headings 9903.01.02...05"*.

## Three parts, each a separate runnable command
1. **Scraper (Hatchet workflow)** — fetch 3 sources: Chapter 99 JSON (~2MB), base schedule chapters 1-97 JSON (~10MB), and the Chapter 99 notes PDF (~14MB) from `hts.usitc.gov`. Land raw payloads in `data/` with provenance (revision tracking — revisions change over time), idempotent, resilient to network failure.
2. **Parser (Hatchet workflow, downstream)** — reads the raw payloads (no network), extracts structure into Postgres: base HTS codes, Chapter 99 rules, and the `references`/`excludes` edges between them (a graph, not a list). Also needs to model the chapter/subchapter notes and link headings to the notes they cite (e.g. "U.S. note 2(a)"), and make rates *computable* (rate_kind + rate_value, since Chapter 99 rates are often additive to a base rate, not absolute).
3. **App (full stack, open-ended)** — something that actually teaches Chapter 99 to a novice, with citations back to source. Precomputation/materialized views encouraged since data only changes on revision.

## Current state of the repo
Completely fresh scaffold — nothing built yet:
- `db/schema.sql` — minimal 3-table starting schema (`hts_base`, `rule`, `rule_edge`), explicitly called a "floor, not a ceiling."
- `workflows/` — only the `echo` demo workflow registered in `worker.py`; Python + `uv`, Hatchet SDK pinned, no HTTP client or PDF parser added yet.
- `app/` — bare Bun/TypeScript scaffold, one route that just lists tables in `chp99`.
- `SUBMISSION.md` — stubbed headings, all empty.
- **Not a git repo yet** (`Is a git repository: false`), and the README says to submit "a git repo (or tarball)."

## Infra
Docker Compose stack: Postgres (`db`), Hatchet Lite (`hatchet`, no-auth dev image, token pre-committed), opt-in `worker` and `app` profiles. `./dev.sh` runs everything with hot reload; `./setup.sh` (re)applies the schema; `./cleanup.sh` wipes volumes.

---

# Part 1 — Scraper

Build a Hatchet workflow that fetches three sources and lands them in durable
storage.

Read [the main README](../README.md) first for background on Chapter 99 and what
we're assessing overall.

---

## The data sources

Three fetches, ~25 MB total:

|     | What                                                   | Size   |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------ |
| 1   | Chapter 99 — the provisions themselves                 | ~2 MB  |
| 2   | Chapters 1–97 — the base schedule Chapter 99 points at | ~10 MB |
| 3   | The Chapter 99 notes PDF                               | ~14 MB |

**1. The Chapter 99 JSON** (~3,300 rows, ~2 MB)

```
https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/exportList?from=9900&to=9999&format=JSON&styles=false
```

**2. The base schedule, chapters 1–97** (~31,900 rows, ~10 MB)

```
https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/exportList?from=0100&to=9799&format=JSON&styles=false
```

**3. The Chapter 99 notes PDF** (~14 MB)

```
https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/file?release=currentRelease&filename=Chapter%2099
```

This is the official chapter document. It contains the tariff table _and_ the
U.S. Notes / Statistical Notes for the chapter and for each subchapter. The notes
are what give the headings their legal meaning.

---

## Requirements

- Fetch all three: Chapter 99, chapters 1–97, and the notes PDF.
- Persist the **raw, unmodified** payloads to `data/` before any parsing. Parsing is lossy
  and your parser will have bugs; you want to re-parse without re-fetching.
- Record enough provenance to answer "where did this row come from, and when?"
  The HTSUS is revised several times a year, and a revision can land mid-exercise.
  As of **2026-08-03** the live release was **Revision 15 (2026)** — the same string
  appears in the PDF header and in `currentRelease` — but treat that as a snapshot,
  not a constant.

  ```bash
  curl -s 'https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/currentRelease'
  # → {"name":"2026HTSRev15","description":"2026 HTS Revision 15","title":"Revision 15 (2026)"}
  ```

- Be idempotent. Running it twice should not corrupt anything or duplicate data.
- Handle errors well, a failure should leave the data in a coherent state.
- Handle failure like the network is real: timeouts, retries with backoff, partial
  success.

---

## Getting started

Hatchet is running from the provided compose file, and `workflows/` already has a
worker plus a workflow that takes an input and returns an output:

```bash
./dev.sh                                       # from the repo root
cd workflows && uv run python -m echo_run "hello"
```

Runs appear at http://localhost:8080 — no login. [`AGENTS.md`](../AGENTS.md) has
the stack in full — services, ports, and how to run the worker on your host
instead — and [`workflows/README.md`](../workflows/README.md) covers the
workflow loop itself.

Hatchet is required here and in [Part 2](PART2_PARSER.md), which is a second
workflow reading what this one writes.

---

Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task. Getting user sign-off on your approach before writing code prevents wasted effort and ensures alignment. This tool transitions you into plan mode where you can explore the codebase and design an implementation approach for user approval.

## When to Use This Tool

**Prefer using EnterPlanMode** for implementation tasks unless they're simple. Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. **New Feature Implementation**: Adding meaningful new functionality
   - Example: "Add a logout button" - where should it go? What should happen on click?
   - Example: "Add form validation" - what rules? What error messages?

2. **Multiple Valid Approaches**: The task can be solved in several different ways
   - Example: "Add caching to the API" - could use Redis, in-memory, file-based, etc.
   - Example: "Improve performance" - many optimization strategies possible

3. **Code Modifications**: Changes that affect existing behavior or structure
   - Example: "Update the login flow" - what exactly should change?

4. **Architectural Decisions**: The task requires choosing between patterns or technologies
   - Example: "Add real-time updates" - WebSockets vs SSE vs polling
   - Example: "Implement state management" - Redux vs Context vs custom solution

5. **Multi-File Changes**: The task will likely touch more than 2-3 files

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the Hatchet Python SDK task retries configuration:

## Task Retries with Backoff Configuration

The Hatchet Python SDK supports task retries with exponential backoff using parameters like `retries` (maximum number of retries), `backoff_max_seconds` (maximum number of seconds to wait between retries), and `backoff_factor` (factor to increase the wait time between retries).

### Example Usage

Here's an example configuration showing a retry sequence: with `backoff_max_seconds=10` and `backoff_factor=2.0`, the wait times between retries follow the sequence 2s, 4s, 8s, 10s, 10s, 10s... due to the maxSeconds limit.

### Client Retry Behavior

By default, the Python SDK retries certain client calls with exponential backoff, with max_attempts defaulting to 5. It's important to note that task retries (which control whether Hatchet retries a task after task failure) are separate from SDK client retries (which control whether the SDK retries certain API calls to Hatchet).

### Best Practices

Remember to use retries judiciously and only for tasks that are idempotent.

For the complete documentation, you can visit the [Hatchet retry policies documentation](https://docs.hatchet.run/v1/retry-policies).

Based on the search results, here's information about timeouts in the Hatchet Python SDK:

## Timeout Parameters

You can specify execution and scheduling timeouts for a task using the `execution_timeout` and `schedule_timeout` parameters when creating a task.

## Timeout Types

Scheduling Timeouts (Default 5m) - the time a task is allowed to wait in the queue before it is cancelled, and Execution Timeouts (Default 60s) - the time a task is allowed to run before it is considered to have failed.

## Timeout Format

In Hatchet, timeouts are specified using a string in the format <number><unit>, where <number> is an integer and <unit> is one of: s, m, or h. If no unit is specified, seconds are assumed.

All times and durations, such as `execution_timeout` and `schedule_timeout`, now allow `datetime.timedelta` objects instead of only allowing strings (e.g. "10s" can be `timedelta(seconds=10)`).

## Task Decorator Usage

Here's an example of using `execution_timeout` with the `@task()` decorator: `@parent_wf.task(execution_timeout=timedelta(minutes=5))`

## Timeout Behavior

If the task is not scheduled before the `schedule_timeout` is reached, it will be cancelled. If the task does not complete before the `execution_timeout` is reached (after starting), it will be cancelled.

# Python SDK Task Retry Configuration

Based on the documentation, here are the exact parameter names for configuring task retries in Python:

## Basic Retries

```python
@simple_workflow.task(retries=3)
def always_fail(input: EmptyModel, ctx: Context) -> dict[str, str]:
    raise Exception("simple task failed")
```

## Exponential Backoff Configuration

```python
@backoff_workflow.task(
    retries=10,
    backoff_max_seconds=10,
    backoff_factor=2.0,
)
def backoff_task(input: EmptyModel, ctx: Context) -> dict[str, str]:
    if ctx.retry_count < 3:
        raise Exception("backoff task failed")
    return {"status": "success"}
```

## Parameter Details

The decorator accepts these parameters:

- **`retries`** (int): Number of retry attempts
- **`backoff_max_seconds`** (int): "Maximum number of seconds to wait between retries"
- **`backoff_factor`** (float): "Factor to increase the wait time between retries"

With these settings, the retry delays follow an exponential sequence (2s, 4s, 8s, 10s, 10s...) constrained by the maximum seconds limit.

input.content:
# Part 1 — Scraper: implementation plan

## Context

Part 1 needs a Hatchet workflow that fetches three USITC sources (Chapter 99
JSON, base schedule JSON for chapters 1-97, and the Chapter 99 notes PDF) and
lands them as raw, unmodified files under `data/`, with enough provenance to
answer "where did this row come from, and when?" It must be idempotent, handle
partial failure without corruption, and retry transient network errors with
backoff. Part 2 (not built yet) will read only from `data/`, never the network,
so everything Part 2 needs must be recoverable from what Part 1 writes to disk.

The repo is currently a fresh scaffold: `workflows/` has only the `echo` demo
workflow, `pyproject.toml` only depends on `hatchet-sdk`, and `data/` is empty
(gitignored except `.gitkeep`). Stack choice already confirmed: Python/`uv` for
workflows, matching the existing scaffold.

Hatchet SDK facts confirmed via docs (docs.hatchet.run) since this is greenfield:
- Task retries/backoff: `@workflow.task(retries=N, backoff_factor=2.0, backoff_max_seconds=60)`.
- Timeouts: `execution_timeout` / `schedule_timeout`, string like `"5m"` or a `timedelta`.
- DAG dependencies: `@workflow.task(parents=[other_task])`, read a parent's result with `ctx.task_output(other_task)`.
- Task decorator param is `input_validator=SomeModel` (matches `echo.py` already).

## Design

**One workflow, five tasks**, all in `workflows/scraper.py`:

```
get_release
    |-- fetch_chapter99      \
    |-- fetch_base_schedule   |--> write_manifest
    |-- fetch_notes_pdf      /
```

- `get_release` — GETs `currentRelease`, returns `{name, description, title}`.
  This makes revision resolution part of the durable, retried, observable run
  instead of something decided once at trigger time.
- `fetch_chapter99`, `fetch_base_schedule`, `fetch_notes_pdf` — each depends
  only on `get_release` (not on each other), so Hatchet runs them concurrently
  and a failure in one doesn't block the other two from landing. Each writes
  one payload file.
- `write_manifest` — fans in on all three fetches. Only runs if all three
  succeeded (Hatchet skips it otherwise), and is the thing that advances
  "latest". This is what keeps a partial failure from leaving `data/` in a
  state Part 2 would mistake for complete.

**On-disk layout** (`DATA_DIR`, env var already wired in `docker-compose.yaml`;
falls back to `<repo>/data` for host runs):

```
data/
  latest.json                        # {"revision": "...", "manifest_path": "...", "updated_at": "..."}
  runs/
    2026HTSRev15/
      chapter99.json
      chapter99.json.meta.json       # sidecar: url, sha256, size, status, fetched_at, duration_ms
      base_schedule.json
      base_schedule.json.meta.json
      chapter99_notes.pdf
      chapter99_notes.pdf.meta.json
      manifest.json                  # revision + all three sidecars, combined
```

Old revision directories are never deleted, so a mid-exercise revision bump
just adds a new directory — history stays inspectable and nothing is lost.

**Idempotency & atomic writes** (`workflows/lib/fetch.py`):
- Each fetch task checks for `<dest>` + `<dest>.meta.json` up front. If both
  exist, skip the network call entirely and reuse the recorded metadata —
  reruns are cheap and don't hammer usitc.gov.
- Otherwise: stream the response to `<dest>.tmp-<uuid>`, hashing (sha256) and
  sizing as it writes. **Validate before committing**: JSON sources must
  `json.loads` successfully and be a non-empty list; the PDF must start with
  the `%PDF-` magic bytes. This stops a 200-status maintenance/error page from
  being silently persisted as if it were good data.
- Only on successful validation: `os.replace(tmp, dest)` (atomic on the same
  filesystem, both POSIX and Windows), then write the `.meta.json` sidecar.
- A stray `.tmp-*` from a previous crash is cleaned up at the start of the
  task, before creating a new one.
- Net effect: a task can be retried, or the whole workflow rerun, any number
  of times, and it converges on the same end state without duplicating or
  corrupting anything.

**Retries / timeouts**: Hatchet task-level retries own all retry/backoff logic
— no nested retry loop inside the task code. `get_release` (`retries=5,
backoff_factor=2.0, backoff_max_seconds=30, execution_timeout="30s"`); each
fetch task (`retries=5, backoff_factor=2.0, backoff_max_seconds=60,
execution_timeout="5m"`, generous enough for the 14 MB PDF on a slow link);
`write_manifest` (`retries=3`). httpx gets its own client-level timeout
(connect/read/write ~10-60s) as a belt-and-suspenders guard against a hung
socket that wouldn't otherwise trip Hatchet's execution timeout quickly.

**`manifest.json`** — the provenance record Part 2 will read:
```json
{
  "revision": {"name": "2026HTSRev15", "description": "...", "title": "..."},
  "generated_at": "2026-09-17T21:10:00Z",
  "sources": {
    "chapter99": {"url": "...", "path": "runs/2026HTSRev15/chapter99.json", "sha256": "...", "size_bytes": ..., "http_status": 200, "fetched_at": "...", "duration_ms": ...},
    "base_schedule": {...},
    "notes_pdf": {...}
  }
}
```
`write_manifest` writes this (atomically, same temp+rename pattern), then
atomically overwrites `data/latest.json` to point at it — the single thing
Part 2 needs to find the newest complete run without touching the network or
scanning directories.

## Files to add/change

- `workflows/scraper.py` — the workflow + 5 tasks described above.
- `workflows/lib/paths.py` — `DATA_DIR` resolution (`DATA_DIR` env var, else `<repo>/data`), revision-dir helper.
- `workflows/lib/fetch.py` — the atomic download-with-validation-and-skip helper, shared by all three fetch tasks.
- `workflows/scraper_run.py` — trigger script mirroring `echo_run.py`: `uv run python -m scraper_run`, blocks for the result, prints revision + per-source size/hash summary, non-zero exit if the run failed.
- `workflows/worker.py` — register `scraper_workflow` alongside (or in place of) `echo_workflow`.
- `workflows/pyproject.toml` — add `httpx`.
- Remove `workflows/echo.py` / `echo_run.py` now that there's a real workflow (per the comment in both files), and trim the now-stale echo walkthrough in `workflows/README.md`.

Nothing touches Postgres or `db/schema.sql` in this part — Part 1's job stops
at `data/`, per the spec ("runnable against payloads fetched an hour ago,
without touching the network" is Part 2's constraint, implying Part 1 doesn't
write to Postgres at all).

## Verification

1. `./dev.sh` from repo root; wait for `hatchet` healthy.
2. `cd workflows && uv sync` (pulls in httpx).
3. `uv run python -m scraper_run` — should print the resolved revision and a
   summary line per source (path, size, sha256 prefix). Check Hatchet UI
   (localhost:8080) for the run and confirm the DAG shape (fan-out from
   `get_release`, fan-in at `write_manifest`).
4. Inspect `data/runs/<revision>/` — all three payload files + sidecars +
   `manifest.json` present; `data/latest.json` points at it.
5. Re-run `uv run python -m scraper_run` — logs should show all three sources
   skipped (cache hit), `manifest.json` regenerated with a new
   `generated_at` but identical file hashes; no duplicate files anywhere.
6. Delete one payload file (not its sidecar) and rerun — confirm the task
   detects the mismatch and re-fetches just that one source, not the other two.
7. Force a failure (e.g. temporarily point one task at a bad path/port) and
   rerun — confirm the other two sources still land, `write_manifest` does not
   run, and `data/latest.json` is untouched; then restore the URL and rerun to
   confirm it heals and completes.

"""Atomic, idempotent, validated downloads.

Every fetch task in the scraper workflow goes through `fetch_with_cache`:
stream to a temp file, hash and size it as it downloads, validate the content
actually looks like what we asked for, then atomically rename into place and
write a metadata sidecar next to it. A file only exists at its final path once
it has been fully downloaded and validated, so a crash or a retry mid-download
can never leave a corrupt or partial payload where Part 2 would find it.

Re-running against a destination that already has both the payload and its
sidecar skips the network call entirely -- reruns are cheap and don't hammer
usitc.gov.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import os
import time
import uuid
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Callable

import httpx

DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = httpx.Timeout(connect=10.0, read=60.0, write=60.0, pool=10.0)


class ValidationError(Exception):
    """Raised when a downloaded payload doesn't look like what we asked for."""


@dataclass
class FetchMeta:
    url: str
    path: str
    sha256: str
    size_bytes: int
    http_status: int
    fetched_at: str
    duration_ms: int
    cached: bool = False

    def to_json(self) -> dict:
        return asdict(self)


def _meta_path(dest: Path) -> Path:
    return dest.with_name(dest.name + ".meta.json")


def _cleanup_stray_temp_files(dest: Path) -> None:
    for stray in dest.parent.glob(f"{dest.name}.tmp-*"):
        stray.unlink(missing_ok=True)


def validate_json_list(path: Path) -> None:
    try:
        with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            data = json.load(f)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        raise ValidationError(f"not valid JSON: {e}") from e
    if not isinstance(data, list) or len(data) == 0:
        raise ValidationError("expected a non-empty JSON array")


def validate_pdf(path: Path) -> None:
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        header = f.read(5)
    if header != b"%PDF-":
        raise ValidationError(f"expected a PDF, got header {header!r}")


def fetch_with_cache(
    client: httpx.Client,
    url: str,
    dest: Path,
    *,
    validate: Callable[[Path], None],
) -> FetchMeta:
    """Download `url` to `dest` unless it's already there (payload + sidecar).

    Returns the metadata sidecar either way, with `cached` set accordingly.
    """
    dest.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    meta_path = _meta_path(dest)

    if dest.exists() and meta_path.exists():
        cached = FetchMeta(**json.loads(meta_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")))
        cached.cached = True
        return cached

    _cleanup_stray_temp_files(dest)
    tmp = dest.with_name(f"{dest.name}.tmp-{uuid.uuid4().hex}")

    started = time.monotonic()
    sha256 = hashlib.sha256()
    size = 0
    status = 0
    try:
        with client.stream("GET", url) as resp:
            resp.raise_for_status()
            status = resp.status_code
            with open(tmp, "wb") as f:
                for chunk in resp.iter_bytes():
                    f.write(chunk)
                    sha256.update(chunk)
                    size += len(chunk)

        validate(tmp)
        os.replace(tmp, dest)
    except Exception:
        tmp.unlink(missing_ok=True)
        raise

    meta = FetchMeta(
        url=url,
        path=str(dest),
        sha256=sha256.hexdigest(),
        size_bytes=size,
        http_status=status,
        fetched_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
        duration_ms=int((time.monotonic() - started) * 1000),
    )
    meta_path.write_text(json.dumps(meta.to_json(), indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    return meta


def atomic_write_json(dest: Path, data: dict) -> None:
    dest.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    tmp = dest.with_name(f"{dest.name}.tmp-{uuid.uuid4().hex}")
    tmp.write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    os.replace(tmp, dest)

"""
The Chapter 99 scraper: fetches the three USITC sources and lands raw,
validated, unmodified payloads under DATA_DIR, with a manifest recording
where each one came from and when.

    uv run python -m scraper_run

See ../parts/PART1_SCRAPER.md for the requirements this satisfies, and
lib/fetch.py for how idempotency and atomicity are implemented.
"""

from datetime import datetime, timezone

import httpx
from hatchet_sdk import Context, Hatchet
from pydantic import BaseModel

from lib.fetch import (
    DEFAULT_TIMEOUT,
    atomic_write_json,
    fetch_with_cache,
    validate_json_list,
    validate_pdf,
)
from lib.paths import LATEST_POINTER, revision_dir

hatchet = Hatchet()

CURRENT_RELEASE_URL = "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/currentRelease"
CHAPTER99_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/exportList?from=9900&to=9999&format=JSON&styles=false"
)
BASE_SCHEDULE_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/exportList?from=0100&to=9799&format=JSON&styles=false"
)
NOTES_PDF_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/file?release=currentRelease&filename=Chapter%2099"
)


class ScraperInput(BaseModel):
    pass


class ReleaseInfo(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str
    title: str


class FetchResult(BaseModel):
    source: str
    url: str
    path: str
    sha256: str
    size_bytes: int
    http_status: int
    fetched_at: str
    duration_ms: int
    cached: bool


class ManifestResult(BaseModel):
    revision: str
    manifest_path: str
    latest_path: str


scraper_workflow = hatchet.workflow(name="Chapter99Scraper", input_validator=ScraperInput)


@scraper_workflow.task(
    retries=5, backoff_factor=2.0, backoff_max_seconds=30, execution_timeout="30s"
)
def get_release(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> ReleaseInfo:
    with httpx.Client(timeout=DEFAULT_TIMEOUT) as client:
        resp = client.get(CURRENT_RELEASE_URL)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        data = resp.json()
    ctx.log(f"current release: {data['name']} ({data['title']})")
    return ReleaseInfo(**data)


def _run_fetch(source: str, url: str, filename: str, validate, ctx: Context) -> FetchResult:
    release = ctx.task_output(get_release)
    dest = revision_dir(release["name"]) / filename
    with httpx.Client(timeout=DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, follow_redirects=True) as client:
        meta = fetch_with_cache(client, url, dest, validate=validate)
    ctx.log(
        f"{source}: {'cached' if meta.cached else 'fetched'} "
        f"{meta.size_bytes} bytes -> {dest}"
    )
    return FetchResult(source=source, **meta.to_json())


@scraper_workflow.task(
    parents=[get_release],
    retries=5,
    backoff_factor=2.0,
    backoff_max_seconds=60,
    execution_timeout="2m",
)
def fetch_chapter99(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> FetchResult:
    return _run_fetch("chapter99", CHAPTER99_URL, "chapter99.json", validate_json_list, ctx)


@scraper_workflow.task(
    parents=[get_release],
    retries=5,
    backoff_factor=2.0,
    backoff_max_seconds=60,
    execution_timeout="5m",
)
def fetch_base_schedule(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> FetchResult:
    return _run_fetch(
        "base_schedule", BASE_SCHEDULE_URL, "base_schedule.json", validate_json_list, ctx
    )


@scraper_workflow.task(
    parents=[get_release],
    retries=5,
    backoff_factor=2.0,
    backoff_max_seconds=60,
    execution_timeout="5m",
)
def fetch_notes_pdf(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> FetchResult:
    return _run_fetch("notes_pdf", NOTES_PDF_URL, "chapter99_notes.pdf", validate_pdf, ctx)


@scraper_workflow.task(
    parents=[get_release, fetch_chapter99, fetch_base_schedule, fetch_notes_pdf],
    retries=3,
)
def write_manifest(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> ManifestResult:
    release = ctx.task_output(get_release)
    sources = {
        "chapter99": ctx.task_output(fetch_chapter99),
        "base_schedule": ctx.task_output(fetch_base_schedule),
        "notes_pdf": ctx.task_output(fetch_notes_pdf),
    }

    manifest_path = revision_dir(release["name"]) / "manifest.json"
    generated_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
    atomic_write_json(
        manifest_path,
        {"revision": release, "generated_at": generated_at, "sources": sources},
    )

    # Only reached once all three fetches succeeded, so this is the one place
    # that advances "latest" -- a partial failure never leaves latest.json
    # pointing at an incomplete run.
    atomic_write_json(
        LATEST_POINTER,
        {
            "revision": release["name"],
            "manifest_path": str(manifest_path),
            "updated_at": generated_at,
        },
    )

    ctx.log(f"manifest written: {manifest_path}")
    return ManifestResult(
        revision=release["name"],
        manifest_path=str(manifest_path),
        latest_path=str(LATEST_POINTER),
    )

validated, unmodified payloads under DATA_DIR, with a manifest recording
where each one came from and when.

    uv run python -m scraper_run

See ../parts/PART1_SCRAPER.md for the requirements this satisfies, and
lib/fetch.py for how idempotency and atomicity are implemented.
"""

from datetime import datetime, timezone

import httpx
from hatchet_sdk import Context, Hatchet
from pydantic import BaseModel

from lib.fetch import (
    DEFAULT_TIMEOUT,
    atomic_write_json,
    fetch_with_cache,
    validate_json_list,
    validate_pdf,
)
from lib.paths import LATEST_POINTER, revision_dir

hatchet = Hatchet()

CURRENT_RELEASE_URL = "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/currentRelease"
CHAPTER99_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/exportList?from=9900&to=9999&format=JSON&styles=false"
)
BASE_SCHEDULE_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/exportList?from=0100&to=9799&format=JSON&styles=false"
)
NOTES_PDF_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/file?release=currentRelease&filename=Chapter%2099"
)


class ScraperInput(BaseModel):
    pass


class ReleaseInfo(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str
    title: str


class FetchResult(BaseModel):
    source: str
    url: str
    path: str
    sha256: str
    size_bytes: int
    http_status: int
    fetched_at: str
    duration_ms: int
    cached: bool


class ManifestResult(BaseModel):
    revision: str
    manifest_path: str
    latest_path: str

    retries=5, backoff_factor=2.0, backoff_max_seconds=30, execution_timeout="30s"
)

    ctx.log(
        f"{source}: {'cached' if meta.cached else 'fetched'} "
        f"{meta.size_bytes} bytes -> {dest}"

    return FetchResult(source=source, **meta.to_json())

# Workflows

Your Hatchet workflows go here. Ships with one that does nothing useful, so you
can confirm the plumbing works before writing the scraper.

## Setup

`./dev.sh` from the repo root runs a worker for you, in a container, and restarts
it when you edit a `.py` here. Trigger a run against it from this directory:

```bash
cd workflows && uv sync
uv run python -m echo_run "hello chapter 99"
# → message='hello chapter 99' length=16
```

To run the worker on your host instead, don't use `./dev.sh` — start just the
infrastructure, then the worker yourself:

```bash
docker compose up -d        # from the repo root; wait for hatchet to be healthy
cd workflows && uv sync
uv run python -m worker     # one terminal: registers workflows, waits for work
uv run python -m echo_run "hello chapter 99"   # another
```

**Run one worker at a time.** They share the token in `.env`, so a host worker
and the container worker will both register and Hatchet will hand tasks to
whichever it picks — including the one running code you didn't just edit.

Runs show up in the Hatchet UI at http://localhost:8080 — no login, it opens
straight to the dashboard. Workflows can be triggered from the UI or
programatically.

## The worker in Docker

`./dev.sh` is the short version. For the worker alone:

```bash
docker compose --profile worker watch    # foreground, restarts on edit
docker compose --profile worker up -d    # detached, no reload
docker compose logs -f worker
```

Either bind-mounts `./workflows`. Under `watch`, editing a `.py` restarts the
worker for you; adding a dependency to `pyproject.toml` restarts it too, picking
up the new package via `uv sync`. Detached, you restart it yourself with
`docker compose restart worker`.

Either path is fine. Host-running gives you a debugger; the container gives you
one less thing to install and the reload for free. Note that from inside the
container your database is `db:5432`, not `localhost:5432` — the service reads
`DATABASE_URL` from the environment for exactly this reason.

## What's here

| File          |                                                             |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `echo.py`     | A workflow with one task: takes an input, returns an output |
| `worker.py`   | The worker process. Register your workflows here            |
| `echo_run.py` | Triggers a run and prints the result                        |
| `.env`        | Hatchet connection settings. Committed — see below          |

## The shape of a workflow

```python
class EchoInput(BaseModel):
    message: str

class EchoOutput(BaseModel):
    message: str
    length: int

echo_workflow = hatchet.workflow(name="Echo", input_validator=EchoInput)

@echo_workflow.task()
def echo(input: EchoInput, ctx: Context) -> EchoOutput:
    return EchoOutput(message=input.message, length=len(input.message))
```

[Hatchet docs](https://docs.hatchet.run/home/setup) is a great resource for
documentation and patterns.

## Notes

**Register your workflows in `worker.py`.** If you forget, the engine will accept
a run and it'll sit queued forever with nothing to pick it up. This is the most
common way to lose ten minutes here.

**The token in `.env` is committed, and that's deliberate.** We run the Hatchet
dev image, which has auth compiled out — no login on the dashboard, and one fixed
non-expiring worker token that's the same on every auth-disabled instance. It
isn't a secret and it survives `./cleanup.sh`, so there's no setup step and
nothing to rotate. Don't copy the pattern into anything real.

# Workflows

Your Hatchet workflows go here.

## Setup

`./dev.sh` from the repo root runs a worker for you, in a container, and restarts
it when you edit a `.py` here. Trigger a run against it from this directory:

```bash
cd workflows && uv sync
uv run python -m scraper_run
```

To run the worker on your host instead, don't use `./dev.sh` — start just the
infrastructure, then the worker yourself:

```bash
docker compose up -d        # from the repo root; wait for hatchet to be healthy
cd workflows && uv sync
uv run python -m worker     # one terminal: registers workflows, waits for work
uv run python -m scraper_run   # another
```

**Run one worker at a time.** They share the token in `.env`, so a host worker
and the container worker will both register and Hatchet will hand tasks to
whichever it picks — including the one running code you didn't just edit.

Runs show up in the Hatchet UI at http://localhost:8080 — no login, it opens
straight to the dashboard. Workflows can be triggered from the UI or
programatically.

## The worker in Docker

`./dev.sh` is the short version. For the worker alone:

```bash
docker compose --profile worker watch    # foreground, restarts on edit
docker compose --profile worker up -d    # detached, no reload
docker compose logs -f worker
```

Either bind-mounts `./workflows`. Under `watch`, editing a `.py` restarts the
worker for you; adding a dependency to `pyproject.toml` restarts it too, picking
up the new package via `uv sync`. Detached, you restart it yourself with
`docker compose restart worker`.

Either path is fine. Host-running gives you a debugger; the container gives you
one less thing to install and the reload for free. Note that from inside the
container your database is `db:5432`, not `localhost:5432` — the service reads
`DATABASE_URL` from the environment for exactly this reason.

## What's here

| File          |                                                             |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `echo.py`     | A workflow with one task: takes an input, returns an output |
| `worker.py`   | The worker process. Register your workflows here            |
| `echo_run.py` | Triggers a run and prints the result                        |
| `.env`        | Hatchet connection settings. Committed — see below          |

## The shape of a workflow

```python
class EchoInput(BaseModel):
    message: str

class EchoOutput(BaseModel):
    message: str
    length: int

echo_workflow = hatchet.workflow(name="Echo", input_validator=EchoInput)

@echo_workflow.task()
def echo(input: EchoInput, ctx: Context) -> EchoOutput:
    return EchoOutput(message=input.message, length=len(input.message))
```

[Hatchet docs](https://docs.hatchet.run/home/setup) is a great resource for
documentation and patterns.

## Notes

**Register your workflows in `worker.py`.** If you forget, the engine will accept
a run and it'll sit queued forever with nothing to pick it up. This is the most
common way to lose ten minutes here.

**The token in `.env` is committed, and that's deliberate.** We run the Hatchet
dev image, which has auth compiled out — no login on the dashboard, and one fixed
non-expiring worker token that's the same on every auth-disabled instance. It
isn't a secret and it survives `./cleanup.sh`, so there's no setup step and
nothing to rotate. Don't copy the pattern into anything real.

Your Hatchet workflows go here.

## Setup

`./dev.sh` from the repo root runs a worker for you, in a container, and restarts

```bash

```

infrastructure, then the worker yourself:

```bash

cd workflows && uv sync
uv run python -m worker     # one terminal: registers workflows, waits for work
uv run python -m scraper_run   # another
```

**Run one worker at a time.** They share the token in `.env`, so a host worker
and the container worker will both register and Hatchet will hand tasks to
whichever it picks — including the one running code you didn't just edit.

Runs show up in the Hatchet UI at http://localhost:8080 — no login, it opens
straight to the dashboard. Workflows can be triggered from the UI or
programatically.

## The worker in Docker

`./dev.sh` is the short version. For the worker alone:

```bash
docker compose --profile worker watch    # foreground, restarts on edit
docker compose --profile worker up -d    # detached, no reload

```

Either bind-mounts `./workflows`. Under `watch`, editing a `.py` restarts the
worker for you; adding a dependency to `pyproject.toml` restarts it too, picking
up the new package via `uv sync`. Detached, you restart it yourself with
`docker compose restart worker`.

Either path is fine. Host-running gives you a debugger; the container gives you
one less thing to install and the reload for free. Note that from inside the
container your database is `db:5432`, not `localhost:5432` — the service reads
`DATABASE_URL` from the environment for exactly this reason.

## What's here

| File              |                                                                |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `scraper.py`      | Part 1: fetches the three USITC sources into `data/`           |
| `scraper_run.py`  | Triggers a scraper run and prints a summary                    |
| `worker.py`       | The worker process. Register your workflows here               |
| `lib/fetch.py`    | Shared atomic-download-with-validation-and-skip helper          |
| `lib/paths.py`    | `DATA_DIR` resolution                                           |
| `.env`            | Hatchet connection settings. Committed — see below              |

## The shape of a workflow

```python
class EchoInput(BaseModel):
    message: str

class EchoOutput(BaseModel):
    message: str
    length: int

echo_workflow = hatchet.workflow(name="Echo", input_validator=EchoInput)

@echo_workflow.task()
def echo(input: EchoInput, ctx: Context) -> EchoOutput:
    return EchoOutput(message=input.message, length=len(input.message))
```

the current HTS revision, three tasks fan out from it to fetch each source in
parallel, and a final task fans back in once all three have landed to write a
manifest. See that file, and `lib/fetch.py`, for how retries, idempotency, and
atomic writes are handled.

[Hatchet docs](https://docs.hatchet.run/home/setup) is a great resource for
documentation and patterns.

## Notes

**Register your workflows in `worker.py`.** If you forget, the engine will accept
a run and it'll sit queued forever with nothing to pick it up. This is the most
common way to lose ten minutes here.

non-expiring worker token that's the same on every auth-disabled instance. It

| `worker.py`       | The worker process. Register your workflows here               |
| `lib/fetch.py`    | Shared atomic-download-with-validation-and-skip helper          |
| `lib/paths.py`    | `DATA_DIR` resolution                                           |
| `.env`            | Hatchet connection settings. Committed — see below              |

## The shape of a workflow

```python
class EchoInput(BaseModel):
    message: str

class EchoOutput(BaseModel):
    message: str
    length: int

echo_workflow = hatchet.workflow(name="Echo", input_validator=EchoInput)

@echo_workflow.task()
def echo(input: EchoInput, ctx: Context) -> EchoOutput:
    return EchoOutput(message=input.message, length=len(input.message))
```

`scraper.py` follows the same shape, with a small DAG: an initial task resolves
the current HTS revision, three tasks fan out from it to fetch each source in
parallel, and a final task fans back in once all three have landed to write a
manifest. See that file, and `lib/fetch.py`, for how retries, idempotency, and
atomic writes are handled.

[Hatchet docs](https://docs.hatchet.run/home/setup) is a great resource for
documentation and patterns.

## Notes

**Register your workflows in `worker.py`.** If you forget, the engine will accept
a run and it'll sit queued forever with nothing to pick it up. This is the most
common way to lose ten minutes here.

**The token in `.env` is committed, and that's deliberate.** We run the Hatchet
dev image, which has auth compiled out — no login on the dashboard, and one fixed
non-expiring worker token that's the same on every auth-disabled instance. It
isn't a secret and it survives `./cleanup.sh`, so there's no setup step and
nothing to rotate. Don't copy the pattern into anything real.

"""
The Chapter 99 scraper: fetches the three USITC sources and lands raw,
validated, unmodified payloads under DATA_DIR, with a manifest recording
where each one came from and when.

    uv run python -m scraper_run

See ../parts/PART1_SCRAPER.md for the requirements this satisfies, and
lib/fetch.py for how idempotency and atomicity are implemented.
"""

from datetime import datetime, timezone

import httpx
from hatchet_sdk import Context, Hatchet
from pydantic import BaseModel

from lib.fetch import (
    DEFAULT_TIMEOUT,
    atomic_write_json,
    fetch_with_cache,
    validate_json_list,
    validate_pdf,
)
from lib.paths import LATEST_POINTER, revision_dir

hatchet = Hatchet()

CURRENT_RELEASE_URL = "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/currentRelease"
CHAPTER99_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/exportList?from=9900&to=9999&format=JSON&styles=false"
)
BASE_SCHEDULE_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/exportList?from=0100&to=9799&format=JSON&styles=false"
)
NOTES_PDF_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/file?release=currentRelease&filename=Chapter%2099"
)


class ScraperInput(BaseModel):
    pass


class ReleaseInfo(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str
    title: str


class FetchResult(BaseModel):
    source: str
    url: str
    path: str
    sha256: str
    size_bytes: int
    http_status: int
    fetched_at: str
    duration_ms: int
    cached: bool


class ManifestResult(BaseModel):
    revision: str
    manifest_path: str
    latest_path: str


scraper_workflow = hatchet.workflow(name="Chapter99Scraper", input_validator=ScraperInput)


@scraper_workflow.task(
    retries=5, backoff_factor=2.0, backoff_max_seconds=30, execution_timeout="30s"
)
def get_release(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> ReleaseInfo:
    with httpx.Client(timeout=DEFAULT_TIMEOUT) as client:
        resp = client.get(CURRENT_RELEASE_URL)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        data = resp.json()
    ctx.log(f"current release: {data['name']} ({data['title']})")
    return ReleaseInfo(**data)


def _run_fetch(source: str, url: str, filename: str, validate, ctx: Context) -> FetchResult:
    release = ctx.task_output(get_release)
    dest = revision_dir(release["name"]) / filename
    with httpx.Client(timeout=DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, follow_redirects=True) as client:
        meta = fetch_with_cache(client, url, dest, validate=validate)
    ctx.log(
        f"{source}: {'cached' if meta.cached else 'fetched'} "
        f"{meta.size_bytes} bytes -> {dest}"
    )
    return FetchResult(source=source, **meta.to_json())


@scraper_workflow.task(
    parents=[get_release],
    retries=5,
    backoff_factor=2.0,
    backoff_max_seconds=60,
    execution_timeout="2m",
)
def fetch_chapter99(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> FetchResult:
    return _run_fetch("chapter99", CHAPTER99_URL, "chapter99.json", validate_json_list, ctx)


@scraper_workflow.task(
    parents=[get_release],
    retries=5,

"""
The Chapter 99 scraper: fetches the three USITC sources and lands raw,
validated, unmodified payloads under DATA_DIR, with a manifest recording
where each one came from and when.

    uv run python -m scraper_run

See ../parts/PART1_SCRAPER.md for the requirements this satisfies, and
lib/fetch.py for how idempotency and atomicity are implemented.
"""

from datetime import datetime, timezone

import httpx
from hatchet_sdk import Context, Hatchet
from pydantic import BaseModel

from lib.fetch import (
    DEFAULT_TIMEOUT,
    atomic_write_json,
    fetch_with_cache,
    validate_json_list,
    validate_pdf,
)
from lib.paths import LATEST_POINTER, revision_dir

hatchet = Hatchet()

CURRENT_RELEASE_URL = "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/currentRelease"
CHAPTER99_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/exportList?from=9900&to=9999&format=JSON&styles=false"
)
BASE_SCHEDULE_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/exportList?from=0100&to=9799&format=JSON&styles=false"
)
NOTES_PDF_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/file?release=currentRelease&filename=Chapter%2099"
)


class ScraperInput(BaseModel):
    pass


class ReleaseInfo(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str
    title: str


class FetchResult(BaseModel):
    source: str
    url: str
    path: str
    sha256: str
    size_bytes: int
    http_status: int
    fetched_at: str
    duration_ms: int
    cached: bool


class ManifestResult(BaseModel):
    revision: str
    manifest_path: str
    latest_path: str


scraper_workflow = hatchet.workflow(name="Chapter99Scraper", input_validator=ScraperInput)


@scraper_workflow.task(
    retries=5, backoff_factor=2.0, backoff_max_seconds=30, execution_timeout="30s"
)
def get_release(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> ReleaseInfo:
    with httpx.Client(timeout=DEFAULT_TIMEOUT) as client:
        resp = client.get(CURRENT_RELEASE_URL)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        data = resp.json()
    ctx.log(f"current release: {data['name']} ({data['title']})")
    return ReleaseInfo(**data)


def _run_fetch(source: str, url: str, filename: str, validate, ctx: Context) -> FetchResult:
    release = ctx.task_output(get_release)
    dest = revision_dir(release.name) / filename
    with httpx.Client(timeout=DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, follow_redirects=True) as client:
        meta = fetch_with_cache(client, url, dest, validate=validate)
    ctx.log(
        f"{source}: {'cached' if meta.cached else 'fetched'} "
        f"{meta.size_bytes} bytes -> {dest}"
    )
    return FetchResult(source=source, **meta.to_json())


@scraper_workflow.task(
    parents=[get_release],
    retries=5,
    backoff_factor=2.0,
    backoff_max_seconds=60,
    execution_timeout="2m",
)
def fetch_chapter99(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> FetchResult:
    return _run_fetch("chapter99", CHAPTER99_URL, "chapter99.json", validate_json_list, ctx)


@scraper_workflow.task(
    parents=[get_release],
    retries=5,
    backoff_factor=2.0,
    backoff_max_seconds=60,
    execution_timeout="5m",
)
def fetch_base_schedule(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> FetchResult:
    return _run_fetch(
        "base_schedule", BASE_SCHEDULE_URL, "base_schedule.json", validate_json_list, ctx
    )


@scraper_workflow.task(
    parents=[get_release],
    retries=5,
    backoff_factor=2.0,
    backoff_max_seconds=60,
    execution_timeout="5m",
)
def fetch_notes_pdf(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> FetchResult:
    return _run_fetch("notes_pdf", NOTES_PDF_URL, "chapter99_notes.pdf", validate_pdf, ctx)


@scraper_workflow.task(
    parents=[get_release, fetch_chapter99, fetch_base_schedule, fetch_notes_pdf],
    retries=3,
)
def write_manifest(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> ManifestResult:
    release = ctx.task_output(get_release)
    sources = {
        "chapter99": ctx.task_output(fetch_chapter99).model_dump(),
        "base_schedule": ctx.task_output(fetch_base_schedule).model_dump(),
        "notes_pdf": ctx.task_output(fetch_notes_pdf).model_dump(),
    }

    manifest_path = revision_dir(release.name) / "manifest.json"
    generated_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
    atomic_write_json(
        manifest_path,
        {"revision": release.model_dump(), "generated_at": generated_at, "sources": sources},
    )

    # Only reached once all three fetches succeeded, so this is the one place
    # that advances "latest" -- a partial failure never leaves latest.json
    # pointing at an incomplete run.
    atomic_write_json(
        LATEST_POINTER,
        {
            "revision": release.name,
            "manifest_path": str(manifest_path),
            "updated_at": generated_at,
        },
    )

    ctx.log(f"manifest written: {manifest_path}")
    return ManifestResult(
        revision=release.name,
        manifest_path=str(manifest_path),
        latest_path=str(LATEST_POINTER),
    )

"""
The Chapter 99 scraper: fetches the three USITC sources and lands raw,
validated, unmodified payloads under DATA_DIR, with a manifest recording
where each one came from and when.

    uv run python -m scraper_run

See ../parts/PART1_SCRAPER.md for the requirements this satisfies, and
lib/fetch.py for how idempotency and atomicity are implemented.
"""

from datetime import datetime, timezone

import httpx
from hatchet_sdk import Context, Hatchet
from pydantic import BaseModel

from lib.fetch import (
    DEFAULT_TIMEOUT,
    atomic_write_json,
    fetch_with_cache,
    validate_json_list,
    validate_pdf,
)
from lib.paths import LATEST_POINTER, revision_dir

hatchet = Hatchet()

CURRENT_RELEASE_URL = "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/currentRelease"
CHAPTER99_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/exportList?from=9900&to=9999&format=JSON&styles=false"
)
BASE_SCHEDULE_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/exportList?from=0100&to=9799&format=JSON&styles=false"
)
NOTES_PDF_URL = (
    "https://hts.usitc.gov/reststop/file?release=currentRelease&filename=Chapter%2099-BROKEN-TEST"
)


class ScraperInput(BaseModel):
    pass


class ReleaseInfo(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str
    title: str


class FetchResult(BaseModel):
    source: str
    url: str
    path: str
    sha256: str
    size_bytes: int
    http_status: int
    fetched_at: str
    duration_ms: int
    cached: bool


class ManifestResult(BaseModel):
    revision: str
    manifest_path: str
    latest_path: str


scraper_workflow = hatchet.workflow(name="Chapter99Scraper", input_validator=ScraperInput)


@scraper_workflow.task(
    retries=5, backoff_factor=2.0, backoff_max_seconds=30, execution_timeout="30s"
)
def get_release(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> ReleaseInfo:
    with httpx.Client(timeout=DEFAULT_TIMEOUT) as client:
        resp = client.get(CURRENT_RELEASE_URL)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        data = resp.json()
    ctx.log(f"current release: {data['name']} ({data['title']})")
    return ReleaseInfo(**data)


def _run_fetch(source: str, url: str, filename: str, validate, ctx: Context) -> FetchResult:
    release = ctx.task_output(get_release)
    dest = revision_dir(release.name) / filename
    with httpx.Client(timeout=DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, follow_redirects=True) as client:
        meta = fetch_with_cache(client, url, dest, validate=validate)
    ctx.log(
        f"{source}: {'cached' if meta.cached else 'fetched'} "
        f"{meta.size_bytes} bytes -> {dest}"
    )
    return FetchResult(source=source, **meta.to_json())


@scraper_workflow.task(
    parents=[get_release],
    retries=5,
    backoff_factor=2.0,
    backoff_max_seconds=60,
    execution_timeout="2m",
)
def fetch_chapter99(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> FetchResult:
    return _run_fetch("chapter99", CHAPTER99_URL, "chapter99.json", validate_json_list, ctx)


@scraper_workflow.task(
    parents=[get_release],
    retries=5,
    backoff_factor=2.0,
    backoff_max_seconds=60,
    execution_timeout="5m",
)
def fetch_base_schedule(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> FetchResult:
    return _run_fetch(
        "base_schedule", BASE_SCHEDULE_URL, "base_schedule.json", validate_json_list, ctx
    )


@scraper_workflow.task(
    parents=[get_release],
    retries=5,
    backoff_factor=2.0,
    backoff_max_seconds=60,
    execution_timeout="5m",
)
def fetch_notes_pdf(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> FetchResult:
    return _run_fetch("notes_pdf", NOTES_PDF_URL, "chapter99_notes.pdf", validate_pdf, ctx)


@scraper_workflow.task(
    parents=[get_release, fetch_chapter99, fetch_base_schedule, fetch_notes_pdf],
    retries=3,
)
def write_manifest(input: ScraperInput, ctx: Context) -> ManifestResult:
    release = ctx.task_output(get_release)
    sources = {
        "chapter99": ctx.task_output(fetch_chapter99).model_dump(),
        "base_schedule": ctx.task_output(fetch_base_schedule).model_dump(),
        "notes_pdf": ctx.task_output(fetch_notes_pdf).model_dump(),
    }

    manifest_path = revision_dir(release.name) / "manifest.json"
    generated_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
    atomic_write_json(
        manifest_path,
        {"revision": release.model_dump(), "generated_at": generated_at, "sources": sources},
    )

    # Only reached once all three fetches succeeded, so this is the one place
    # that advances "latest" -- a partial failure never leaves latest.json
    # pointing at an incomplete run.
    atomic_write_json(
        LATEST_POINTER,
        {
            "revision": release.name,
            "manifest_path": str(manifest_path),
            "updated_at": generated_at,
        },
    )

    ctx.log(f"manifest written: {manifest_path}")
    return ManifestResult(
        revision=release.name,
        manifest_path=str(manifest_path),
        latest_path=str(LATEST_POINTER),
    )

## 1. How to run it

<!--

We will follow these literally, so include the setup steps you'd otherwise do

-->

### Part 1 — Scraper

```bash
./dev.sh                                   # from repo root; brings up db, hatchet, worker, app
cd workflows && uv sync
uv run python -m scraper_run
```

What you should see: the current HTS revision (e.g. `revision=2026HTSRev19`),
then one line per source (`chapter99`, `base_schedule`, `notes_pdf`) showing
`fetched` or `cached`, its size, and a sha256 prefix. On disk:

```
data/latest.json                       # points at the newest complete run
data/runs/<revision>/chapter99.json
data/runs/<revision>/base_schedule.json
data/runs/<revision>/chapter99_notes.pdf
data/runs/<revision>/*.meta.json       # per-source fetch provenance
data/runs/<revision>/manifest.json     # revision + all three sources' provenance, combined
```

Safe to run repeatedly: a source already on disk (payload + its `.meta.json`
sidecar both present) is skipped rather than re-fetched. `manifest.json` /
`data/latest.json` are only (re)written once all three sources for that run
have succeeded, so a partial failure can't advance "latest" or look complete.
Verified by hand: killing one source mid-run leaves the other two on disk and
`data/latest.json` untouched; rerunning afterward heals it (re-fetches only
the missing/failed source, reuses the rest, then completes the manifest).
